passage:
"Look at her. Twenty-one, like me. Perfect skin, a flat in Goa, a job she loves."
"Sarita, it's midnight. Put the phone down."
"No, look, Rashmi. And the ad right under it: 'Glass skin in 14 days.' I'm ordering it."
"You said your skin was fine last week."
"That was before I saw this. I feel like I'm so behind. Everyone's living a life and I'm in a hostel eating instant noodles."
"Zoom into her hand."
"...Why is the door frame bending?"
"Because the photo is edited. Half of what you're looking at doesn't exist."
"But the serum..."
"The serum ad sits under the edited photo on purpose. First they make you feel behind, then they sell you the fix."
Sarita put the phone face down.
"I still feel a bit rubbish."
"I know. Come make chai with me."

qa.q: What does the serum ad promise?
qa.a: The serum ad promises "Glass skin in 14 days".

qa.q: What is Sarita feeling while scrolling?
qa.a: Sarita feels behind and insecure, saying everyone else is living a life while Sarita is stuck in a hostel eating noodles.

qa.q: What helped Sarita step back from ordering?
qa.a: Rashmi got Sarita to zoom in on the bent door frame, which showed the photo was edited, and named how the ad was placed to use that feeling.

qa.q: How does Rashmi see the post differently from Sarita?
qa.a: Rashmi sees the post and ad as a sales pair that first creates a feeling of lack and then offers the fix, rather than as a real life to measure against.

grounding: A young adult comparing their life to edited photos feels behind and nearly buys a serum, until Rashmi shows how the ad uses that insecurity.

passage:
I spent most of last winter feeling like my life was a draft and everyone else's was the final copy.
Every morning I scrolled through people my age with white bedsheets, sunlit desks and planners full of neat handwriting. Under almost every post there was an ad: the lamp, the linen, the planner. By January I had bought all three. My room still looked like my room. I felt worse, like even the fix hadn't worked on me.
Then Naveen from my design class sent me two photos of his own desk: one "for posting", with warm light and one plant carefully placed, and one real, with chargers and a cold cup of tea.
"Same desk," he wrote. "Ten minutes apart."
I laughed for the first time in weeks. The planner is now half empty. The lamp is nice, honestly.
Pooja

qa.q: What three things did the narrator buy by January?
qa.a: Pooja bought the lamp, the linen and the planner.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel after buying all three things?
qa.a: Pooja felt disappointed and even lower than before, as if even the fix had failed, because the room still did not look like the posts.

qa.q: What was the turning point that changed how Pooja saw the posts?
qa.a: Naveen's two photos of the same desk, one set up for posting and one real, showed how much the polished images were staged.

qa.q: Why might Naveen have chosen to share his own messy desk?
qa.a: Naveen likely wanted to show Pooja that the perfect images are arranged, and sharing his own real desk made that point kindly without a lecture.

grounding: A young adult feels behind after polished lifestyle posts with ads beneath them, buys the products, and feels no better until shown how posts are staged.

passage:
You know what, Sahil, I'll tell you, because you're the one who noticed I stopped coming for chai.
It's me, Lokesh, the guy who used to laugh at gym selfies. Last semester my feed turned into shirtless guys on beaches, all glowing, captions like "Stop making excuses." Then the ads: a twelve-week programme, a tub of powder, "Your new life starts now."
I'd look at myself in the hostel mirror at night and feel like I was already behind at twenty. Everyone had a body, a trip, a startup. I had a mess tray.
The programme was in my cart when my cousin sent me a behind-the-scenes clip from a shoot: lights, a quick workout right before the photos, then editing. Same guy, ordinary shoulders.
I deleted the cart and unfollowed forty accounts. I still feel it sometimes. But now I notice the ad shows up exactly when I'm feeling worst.

qa.q: What was in Lokesh's cart when the cousin's clip arrived?
qa.a: The programme was in the cart.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel looking in the hostel mirror at night?
qa.a: Lokesh felt insecure and behind, as if everyone else had a body, a trip and a startup while Lokesh had only a mess tray.

qa.q: What steps helped Lokesh, and what else could help?
qa.a: Seeing the behind-the-scenes clip, deleting the cart and unfollowing forty accounts; talking to a friend like Sahil when the feeling returns can help too.

qa.q: How might Sahil have seen Lokesh during that semester?
qa.a: Sahil noticed Lokesh had stopped coming for chai, so from outside it looked like pulling away from friends, not a shopping decision.

grounding: Shows a young adult made to feel behind by polished bodies and lifestyle posts, with ads offering a programme as the answer to that insecurity.

passage:
Week one: Rafiq kept pausing on the same reels, old school friends at weddings with skin smooth as glass. Under every third reel came an ad: "Tired of dull skin? Glow in 7 days." He touched the marks on his cheek in the bus window and felt twenty going on forty.
Week two, a Thursday: At 2 am he ordered the glow kit, a cleanser, a serum and a cream. The relief lasted until breakfast.
Week five, a Sunday: Wasim was editing their photos from a cousin's engagement. "Watch," he said, and slid one bar. Rafiq's marks vanished. He slid another, and Wasim's own jaw sharpened. "That's what everyone's doing."
Rafiq laughed, surprised at how much lighter he felt. The kit sat half-used on the shelf. That evening he muted the reels from his school friends.

qa.q: What did the ad under every third reel say?
qa.a: 'Tired of dull skin? Glow in 7 days.'

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he touched the marks on his cheek?
qa.a: Rafiq felt self-conscious and behind, comparing his skin with the smooth, polished faces in the reels.

qa.q: What small step did Rafiq take at the end, and why could it help?
qa.a: Rafiq muted the reels from his school friends, which cuts down the comparisons the ads were feeding on.

qa.q: What was it like for Wasim to show how the editing works?
qa.a: Wasim treated it lightly, even sharpening his own jaw, which let Rafiq see that everyone polishes photos without feeling judged.

grounding: Shows a young adult feeling behind after edited photos and a skin-glow ad, buying the kit, then seeing how editing creates the polish.

passage:
Come, Elizabeth, sit. You've been scrolling those holiday photos all lunch with a long face. Let me tell you something from when I was about your age, twenty-one, in a hostel in Pune.
We had no phones, but we had magazines. Every page: a man in a white shirt on a motorbike, people laughing around him, and a bottle of aftershave. "Be the man they notice." I had one good shirt and a bicycle with no brakes.
I saved my canteen money for two months and bought that aftershave. My roommate Mani watched me splash it on for a college function. Nobody noticed. It gave me a rash.
Mani said, "Uday, the fellow in the ad is a model. They paid him. They didn't pay you." I was angry for a day. Then we laughed about it for thirty years.
That ad wasn't selling a smell. It was selling the feeling I didn't have.

qa.q: What did the magazine ads say beside the aftershave?
qa.a: 'Be the man they notice.'

qa.q: How did young Uday feel looking at those magazine ads?
qa.a: Young Uday felt insecure and left behind, with one good shirt and a bicycle with no brakes next to the men on motorbikes.

qa.q: What turning point inside the story changed how Uday saw the aftershave?
qa.a: Mani's words that the man in the ad was a paid model; after a day of anger, Uday could see the ad was selling a missing feeling, not a smell.

qa.q: What might Mani have been feeling while watching Uday splash on the aftershave?
qa.a: Mani was probably fond but concerned, watching a friend spend two months' canteen money chasing an ad, and chose honesty over flattery.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how ads for a polished lifestyle worked on his insecurity at twenty-one, selling a product as the answer.

passage: It was 1 a.m. in exam week, and Minakshi should have been revising microbiology. Instead she was scrolling. A girl her age on a rooftop in Goa, skin glowing, captioned "my morning routine". Then an ad: "Tired of dull skin? Our 5-step glow kit, 40% off tonight." Then another girl, another beach. Minakshi caught her reflection in the dark screen: spots from stress, hair tied with a rubber band. Everyone else seemed to have their lives sorted. She had just enough money left for the month's bus pass, and her thumb hovered over Buy now. Zainab, her flatmate, padded in for water and saw the screen. "That one," she said, tapping the rooftop girl. "I follow her too. She posted last month that she uses three filters and a ring light. And the kit company pays her." Minakshi laughed, a little shakily. She closed the app, put the phone face down, and opened her microbiology notes.

qa.q: What did the ad offer?
qa.a: A 5-step glow kit, 40% off tonight.

qa.q: How was Minakshi feeling while scrolling?
qa.a: Minakshi felt behind and insecure, comparing her stress spots and rubber-band hair with glowing, sorted lives.

qa.q: What helped Minakshi step back?
qa.a: Zainab pointed out the filters, the ring light and the paid deal, which showed the polished image was edited and selling; Minakshi then closed the app.

qa.q: How might Zainab see these posts?
qa.a: Zainab sees them with a clearer eye, knowing about filters and sponsorship, and wants to protect Minakshi from buying out of insecurity.

grounding: Shows a young adult comparing herself with edited photos and ads for glowing skin late at night, with the product sold as the answer.
